pos: n. (the head of a family that returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel)
etymology: Hebrew Zakkai (H2140), from zakak (H2141), to be clear, pure, or bright.
biblical_def: Zaccai heads one of the larger returning households in both censuses of the return: “The children of Zaccai, seven hundred and threescore” (Ezra 2:9), preserved word for word in Nehemiah’s independently drawn register, “The children of Zaccai, seven hundred and threescore” (Nehemiah 7:14). The two counts agree exactly, unlike a number of the neighboring households whose figures differ by one or two between the two books — a small but real mark that this particular record was transmitted with unusual care, whatever the cause. The Hebrew root behind the name means clear, pure, or bright, the same root family that gives the adjective translated pure or clean elsewhere in the Old Testament. A household of over seven hundred souls, named for purity, is counted among those who “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1) and were at last settled among “all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70) — a large company brought home clean out of a captivity that was itself, in the prophets’ own reckoning, chastening for uncleanness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Zaccai; the Hebrew root means clear, pure, or bright, and the name belongs to a large household counted identically at seven hundred and threescore in both Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s registers.

PURE, a. Clear; free from mixture; unadulterated; free from moral defilement.
CLEAR, a. Free from cloud, obscurity, or dimness; free from guilt or blame.
CENSUS, n. An official enumeration of the inhabitants of a country or province.
REMNANT, n. That which remains after a part is separated, removed, or destroyed.

Ezra 2:70

corruption_summary: A large household counted with unusual exactness across two independent registers is exactly the kind of detail a careless-redaction theory of the historical books cannot easily account for.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical reconstructions that treat Ezra and Nehemiah as loosely assembled from disagreeing sources tend to fasten on the numbers that differ between the two censuses and pass over, in silence, the many that agree exactly, of which Zaccai’s seven hundred and threescore is a clear example. A theory built only on the discrepancies, while ignoring the far larger body of exact agreement, is not reading the evidence fairly; it is reading for the conclusion it already wants.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD numbers His people not as an undifferentiated mass but household by household, and that purity of name is no guarantee of purity of heart — the same captivity that scattered this large, cleanly named household was itself the LORD’s own chastening of an unclean people. Return did not erase the need for holiness; it renewed the occasion for it.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon; spelled Bazlith in Nehemiah's parallel register)
etymology: Hebrew Batsluth / Batslith (H1213), from the same root as H1211, betsel, an onion or a peeling; the name suggests a peeling or stripping away.
biblical_def: Bazluth names a family of Nethinim listed among the returning exiles: “The children of Bazluth, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha” (Ezra 2:52). Nehemiah’s parallel and independently kept register preserves the household at the same place with a slightly shortened spelling: “The children of Bazlith, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha” (Nehemiah 7:54). Strong’s concordance connects the name to the same Hebrew root as betsel, an onion, and to the idea of peeling or stripping away an outer layer. Scripture gives no story behind the name beyond its place in the register; it stands among the Nethinim, the servants given to the daily work of the temple, one household in a long column of households, distinguished from its neighbors only by this one word. The frame the Chronicler puts around the whole list supplies the theology the name itself withholds: a people once stripped bare by exile “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1).

corruption_summary: A minor spelling shift between Bazluth and Bazlith across two parallel registers is sometimes cited as manuscript instability; it is ordinary transliteration variance within a single honestly transmitted record.
corruption_paragraphs: As with several households in this same section of the list, a critical reading eager to find fault treats the shortened Nehemiah spelling as evidence the two books cannot be reconciled into one reliable history. The far simpler and more common explanation, attested throughout ancient Near Eastern administrative documents generally, is that proper names carried minor spelling variation even within a single scribal culture, and neither biblical author felt any need to standardize the other's form.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the root itself: a name connected to peeling or stripping away belongs to a household that had, in fact, been stripped of land, temple, and inheritance by exile, and was given all of it back by the same sovereign hand that had first stripped it away.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Mechida, of uncertain derivation, possibly connected to chidah (H2420), a riddle or dark saying.
biblical_def: Mehida names a family of Nethinim recorded between two other households in both censuses of the return: “The children of Bazluth, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha” (Ezra 2:52), matched in Nehemiah’s independent register, “The children of Bazlith, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha” (Nehemiah 7:54). The derivation of the name is genuinely uncertain; some lexicons connect it distantly to the Hebrew word for a riddle or a dark saying, though this cannot be pressed with confidence. What is certain is the household’s place among the Nethinim, the servants given to the daily labor of the temple, carried into captivity and carried home again by name. Scripture is willing, in a list like this, to preserve a name whose meaning even careful readers cannot now recover with certainty — the record does not require that every detail be explicable to be trustworthy. The household is set within the same frame as its neighbors: “every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), and at the last, “all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70).

corruption_summary: An uncertain etymology is sometimes filled in by popular online sources with confident but invented meanings; sound lexicography says plainly when a derivation is not known rather than manufacturing false certainty.
corruption_paragraphs: Much internet Bible-name material assigns a tidy, confident gloss to every name in Scripture, including names whose Hebrew root is genuinely disputed among serious lexicographers, simply because a definite-sounding answer is more shareable than an honest admission of uncertainty. This dictionary would rather say a derivation is uncertain than invent a meaning to satisfy the reader’s appetite for tidiness.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD’s knowledge of His people does not depend on our ability to etymologize their names. What is uncertain to the modern reader was never uncertain to Him; He called Mehida’s house by name out of Babylon whether or not later ages could recover what the name first meant.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Charsha, from charash (H2790), to engrave, to plow, or to devise silently; a name suggesting a craftsman or silent worker.
biblical_def: Harsha closes the same short household group in both censuses of the return: “The children of Bazluth, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha” (Ezra 2:52), preserved identically in Nehemiah’s parallel record, “The children of Bazlith, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha” (Nehemiah 7:54). The Hebrew root behind the name, charash, carries a striking double sense in the Old Testament: it names a craftsman who engraves or works skillfully with his hands, and it also means to be silent, to hold one’s peace. A household bearing this name returned to a city still lying in ruins, its walls broken down, waiting on exactly the kind of skilled, silent labor the root suggests — the same patient craft Nehemiah would soon call for at the wall itself. The record gives no more than the name and the number, set within the list’s own frame: they “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), among “all Israel in their cities” (Nehemiah 7:73).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Harsha; the Hebrew root can mean either a skilled craftsman or to be silent, and the name belongs to a family of Nethinim recorded identically in both Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s registers.

corruption_summary: The double sense of the root, craftsman and silence, is worth naming precisely rather than collapsing into a single vague gloss, as popular sources are prone to do with any Hebrew root that carries more than one meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: A shallow handling of Hebrew etymology tends to pick whichever sense of a root sounds most interesting and present it as the settled meaning, when in fact charash genuinely carries both senses across its Old Testament occurrences, craft and silence together, and a responsible dictionary names both rather than flattening the word for a cleaner headline.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of quiet, skilled work. A returning people rebuilding a ruined city needed craftsmen more than orators, and a household named for exactly that combination — skilled hands, a silent tongue — is as fitting a name as any in the whole register for the work Nehemiah’s generation was about to undertake.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Barqos (H1302), of uncertain derivation, possibly connected to a root for variegated color or embroidery.
biblical_def: Barkos heads a household of Nethinim listed beside two others in both censuses of the return: “The children of Barkos, the children of Sisera, the children of Thamah” (Ezra 2:53), matched in Nehemiah’s parallel register with one name spelled slightly differently, “The children of Barkos, the children of Sisera, the children of Tamah” (Nehemiah 7:55). The second name in the group, Sisera, is a striking one: it is the same Hebrew name borne by the Canaanite general whom Deborah and Barak routed and whom Jael slew with a tent peg (Judges 4–5), yet here it names an unrelated household of temple servants generations later. This entry is on Barkos, not Sisera, and the two are not the same person or house; Scripture’s own habit of reusing a name across very different men and centuries is on full display in this one short verse, and the reader is meant to read each occurrence on its own terms. Barkos’s own derivation is uncertain, but his household’s place is not: among the Nethinim who “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1).

corruption_summary: A shared name between a temple-servant household and the Canaanite general Sisera is sometimes mistaken by careless readers for the same entity; Scripture, read plainly, identifies neither with the other, and this entry keeps them separate.
corruption_paragraphs: Amateur Bible-name searches that simply match a string of letters across the whole concordance can easily conflate two entirely unrelated men across five centuries because they happen to share a Hebrew name, producing a garbled composite figure that the text itself never intends. Careful reading requires attending to the historical context of each occurrence, not merely the spelling.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that names are not destinies and are not even unique identifiers in Scripture; the same word can belong to an enemy of Israel in one century and to a servant of the temple in another. What determines a man’s place before the LORD is never his name but his standing in the covenant.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Netsiach (H5335), from natsach (H5329), to be conspicuous, preeminent, or enduring; the same root behind the musical term translated “to the chief Musician” in the Psalms.
biblical_def: Neziah names a family of Nethinim recorded at the close of a short group in both censuses of the return: “The children of Neziah, the children of Hatipha” (Ezra 2:54), preserved word for word in Nehemiah’s independent register, “The children of Neziah, the children of Hatipha” (Nehemiah 7:56). This is one of the shortest verses in either list, only two households, and yet the two registers agree in it precisely. The Hebrew root behind Neziah’s name, natsach, means to be conspicuous, preeminent, or enduring, and is the very word rendered “to the chief Musician” over dozens of the Psalms — a title for the one appointed to oversee and preserve the song for lasting use. A household of temple servants bearing a name built on enduring preeminence returned to serve, however humbly, at the house where that same root word headed the Psalter’s own songs of praise. The census frame supplies the rest: “every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), among “all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70).

corruption_summary: A brief, two-name verse repeated identically in both registers is easy to pass over as trivial; it is in fact one of the plainer proofs in the chapter of how faithfully the record was kept.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be simple for a source-critical reading to treat so short and minor a verse as filler, evidence that the list was padded to inflate the appearance of a large and orderly return. But padding does not typically reproduce itself word for word across two independently compiled books decades apart in their final form; exact, minimal agreement of this kind is the signature of careful transmission, not embellishment.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD’s preservation of His people extends even to the smallest, most easily overlooked households — a name meaning conspicuous or enduring, attached to a family that would otherwise have vanished from history in two bare Hebrew words, endures still because Scripture chose to record it.

pos: n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Chatipha, from chataph (H2414), to seize, to snatch, to catch away by force.
biblical_def: Hatipha closes the same short two-household verse in both censuses of the return: “The children of Neziah, the children of Hatipha” (Ezra 2:54), repeated identically in Nehemiah’s independent register, “The children of Neziah, the children of Hatipha” (Nehemiah 7:56). The Hebrew root behind the name, chataph, means to seize or to snatch away by force — a plain, almost blunt description of exactly what had happened to this household and to every household in the list. Nebuchadnezzar had snatched Judah from its land; the name Hatipha may simply record, in one word, what an entire generation had suffered. Scripture does not dwell on the violence of the name; it lets it stand beside its neighbor Neziah, conspicuous and enduring, and moves on to the next household, as though to say that even a name built on being seized away belongs, in the end, to a people who “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Hatipha; the Hebrew root means to seize or snatch away by force, a fitting description of the captivity itself, and the name belongs to a family of Nethinim recorded identically in both registers.

corruption_summary: A name built on the plain violence of being seized away is real history, not a metaphor to be softened into a more comfortable therapeutic vocabulary of loss or displacement.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern sensibilities are quick to reframe every biblical account of conquest and deportation in the softer vocabulary of trauma and displacement, which, while not wrong to name real suffering, can quietly relocate the moral center of the account from the LORD's righteous judgment on covenant unfaithfulness to a generalized narrative of victimhood detached from sin and repentance. The Chronicler himself is not so delicate; he names Nebuchadnezzar as the one the LORD sent, and Hatipha's own name preserves the blunt fact of being seized.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD who allowed His people to be seized away in righteous judgment is the same LORD who brought a household bearing that very name back to its own city. Judgment and restoration are not opposites in the biblical record; they are two acts of the same sovereign hand.

pos: n. (a family of the servants of Solomon who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Chattil, of uncertain derivation, possibly from a root meaning to waver, to be talkative, or to babble.
biblical_def: Hattil names a household grouped among the children of Solomon’s servants in both censuses of the return: “The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Ami” (Ezra 2:57), matched in Nehemiah’s independent register with one variant name in the same list, “The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Amon” (Nehemiah 7:59). This group is distinguished in the surrounding text from the Nethinim proper; they descend from men whom Solomon himself had set to serve the temple generations earlier, a class of servant whose origin reached back to the height of Israel’s glory under its wisest king and whose descendants now returned in humbled obscurity from Babylon. Whatever wavering or uncertain root the name Hattil carries, the household’s course did not waver: it is counted, twice, among those who “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Hattil; the derivation is uncertain, and the name belongs to a household of the servants of Solomon whose descendants returned from Babylonian captivity generations after the kingdom’s glory had passed.

NETHINIM, n. Those given; temple servants assigned to assist the Levites.

corruption_summary: The descent of Solomon's servants into a small, obscure household four centuries later is sometimes read by moderns as tragic decline; Scripture reads it as ordinary providence, neither glorifying the ancestor's grandeur nor lamenting the descendant's obscurity.
corruption_paragraphs: A romanticized, progress-obsessed reading of history wants every generation to exceed the last, and so treats a household's fall from serving under Solomon's golden temple to serving under Zerubbabel's much smaller second temple as a story of tragic decline needing to be mourned or explained away. Scripture itself records the transition without editorial lament; Haggai and Zechariah both address the smallness of the second temple directly and promise the LORD's presence in it regardless of its diminished glory.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faithfulness in a smaller house is not a lesser thing before the LORD than service in a grander one. The children of Solomon's servants who returned to a modest, rebuilt temple were no less counted among the LORD's people than their ancestors who had served under a king's full splendor.

pos: n. (a family of the servants of Solomon who returned from Babylon, further identified as "of Zebaim")
etymology: Hebrew Pokereth, feminine participle from pakhar, to catch, to snare; possibly an occupational name for a gazelle-catcher or fowler, joined to the place-name Zebaim.
biblical_def: Pochereth names a household counted among the children of Solomon’s servants: “The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Ami” (Ezra 2:57), preserved at the same place in Nehemiah’s independent register: “The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Amon” (Nehemiah 7:59). The name is unusual among this whole list for carrying its own place-name attached, “of Zebaim,” likely marking the household’s town of origin before the exile, the only such double naming in this section of the register. The Hebrew root behind Pochereth suggests catching or snaring, possibly an ancestral trade of hunting or fowling, feminized in form, perhaps preserving an ancestress’s name at the head of the house rather than an ancestor’s. Whatever the household’s trade or origin, it is counted among those who “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), a trade-name and a town-name both carried home together.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Pochereth; the Hebrew root suggests catching or snaring, in a feminine form, joined to the place-name Zebaim, and belongs to a household of Solomon's servants who returned from Babylon.

corruption_summary: A feminine-formed occupational name is a small, honest detail of the ancient record, not a doctrinal statement about women's roles one way or the other; it should not be pressed into service of a modern argument it was never meant to carry.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be an overreach in either direction to build a large theological argument on a single obscure genealogical name, whether to claim it proves matriarchal household leadership was normative in Israel or, conversely, to explain it away rather than simply noting the grammatical form honestly. The dictionary's complementarian conviction rests on the plain, repeated teaching of Scripture concerning the order of creation and the church, not on genealogical trivia, and this entry treats the name as exactly what it is: one household's inherited designation, feminine in form, of unknown further significance.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary dignity of a working household’s trade being remembered by name across a captivity and a return, whatever ancestor, man or woman, first bore it. The LORD’s record-keeping does not depend on the modern reader being able to reconstruct every detail of a family's internal history.

pos: n. (a family of the servants of Solomon who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Darqon (H1874), of uncertain derivation, possibly connected to derek (H1870), a way or a path.
biblical_def: Darkon names a household among the children of Solomon’s servants returning from Babylon: “The children of Jaalah, the children of Darkon, the children of Giddel” (Ezra 2:56), preserved at the same place in Nehemiah’s independent register with a minor spelling difference in its neighbor, “The children of Jaala, the children of Darkon, the children of Giddel” (Nehemiah 7:58). Some lexicons connect the name to the ordinary Hebrew word for a way or a path, the same root that gives the familiar phrase “the way of the LORD” throughout the Psalms and Prophets, though the connection cannot be pressed with certainty for a name this rare. Whatever its exact sense, a household possibly named for a path undertook the longest and most consequential path of its generation, out of Babylon and back to Jerusalem, and is recorded among those who “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), settled at last among “all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Darkon; some lexicons connect the name to the Hebrew word for a way or path, and it belongs to a household of Solomon's servants who returned from Babylonian captivity.

corruption_summary: A speculative etymology connecting an obscure name to a common root is worth stating cautiously, as this entry does, rather than as settled fact the way popular online sources routinely overstate uncertain derivations.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting, once a plausible root is found for a rare name, to state the connection with more confidence than the linguistic evidence actually supports; this entry names the possibility while being honest that the name is too rare in the text to confirm it beyond doubt, a discipline too many popular reference works abandon in favor of a more satisfying, tidy answer.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every household in this register walked one concrete, physical way — the actual road from Babylon to Jerusalem — and that the LORD who is Himself called the Way for His people ordered that road home for households no more remarkable than this one.
